analysis.one_liner: Repeals the Affordable Care Act automatically if enrollment in its new health insurance marketplaces falls short of 7 million people.
analysis.headline: The bill had no cosponsors, never got a hearing or vote in any of its eight committees, and died when the 113th Congress ended in January 2015.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required the Comptroller General to certify by June 1, 2014 whether at least 7 million people had enrolled in health plans through the ACA's exchanges by March 31, 2014. If that number was not met, the Affordable Care Act and its related reconciliation law provisions would be repealed retroactive to their 2010 enactment — meaning the new marketplaces, subsidies, Medicaid expansion, and protections like the ban on denying coverage for pre-existing conditions would all vanish at once. The bill never advanced past committee referral.
analysis.who_benefits: Had it passed and the trigger been met, the main beneficiaries would have been people who opposed the ACA's individual mandate and wanted the law's requirements, subsidies, and regulations ended outright — along with those who pay for health coverage entirely on their own and bore the law's costs. No one would have gained a replacement program; the bill repealed, it did not replace.

how_it_helps.text: For its supporters, the bill offered a path to end the individual mandate and the rest of the ACA if exchange enrollment fell short of the 7 million goal, using an enrollment miss as the legal trigger for repeal.

analysis.who_pays: If the trigger had been hit, the cost would have fallen on millions of people who had just gained coverage or affordability help through the ACA: subsidized exchange enrollees, adults covered by the Medicaid expansion, and anyone with a pre-existing condition who again faced denial or surcharges. Insurers selling exchange plans and hospitals serving newly uninsured patients would also have lost.
analysis.who_pays_short: ACA enrollees and people with pre-existing conditions

drawbacks.text: The trigger was all-or-nothing and retroactive: missing a single 7 million enrollment target would have repealed the entire ACA — including Medicaid expansion, protections for pre-existing conditions, and subsidies — even for the millions who had already signed up.

The bill offered no replacement coverage or transition plan, so if the trigger hit, people who had purchased plans or newly qualified for Medicaid would have lost coverage with no alternative in place.

The 7 million figure was an administration projection, not a statutory requirement of the ACA, so the bill tied the fate of the whole law to a benchmark that did not determine whether the law was working.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: As written, the bill's cost would have fallen hardest on ordinary people: repealing the ACA because sign-ups lagged a fixed 7 million target would have taken coverage away from millions who had enrolled and from Medicaid-eligible adults, and ended protections for pre-existing conditions, all based on a single enrollment snapshot from the law's troubled first weeks. Its benefit was framed as relieving people of the individual mandate penalty, but the repeal trigger was automatic and all-or-nothing, with no transition or replacement plan. On balance the drawbacks far outweighed the benefit.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in December 2013, referred to eight House committees, and sat in a subcommittee until the Congress ended, with no cosponsors and no vote ever taken.

narrative.text: Rep. Ted Yoho introduced the NUMBER Act on December 19, 2013, during the first open enrollment period of the ACA.
The bill was referred to eight House committees and then to two subcommittees; no committee reported it out and the full House never considered it.
It drew no cosponsors, reflecting the absence of visible support beyond the sponsor.
The bill expired when the 113th Congress ended on January 3, 2015.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: People who rely on the ACA — subsidized enrollees, Medicaid expansion recipients, and those with pre-existing conditions — were better off, because their coverage was not put at risk; no concentrated interest gained anything, since nothing happened.

for.name: Rep. Ted Yoho
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and gave it its only momentum; no other member cosponsored it.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had a single Republican sponsor, no cosponsors of any party, and no recorded votes; it never drew enough support to reach the floor.

industries.note: If the trigger had been met, repeal would have ended the exchange marketplaces and the subsidies that channel customers to insurers, eliminating the ACA-guaranteed individual market. Since the bill died, insurers kept the ACA marketplaces. Had it passed, millions of subsidized customers would have disappeared.
The bill died, so providers continued to receive payments tied to ACA coverage expansion; had repeal triggered, uncompensated care from newly uninsured patients would have grown.

industries.industry: Uninsured households and people with pre-existing conditions
industries.note: A repeal trigger would have ended the subsidies and rules that made coverage affordable and guaranteed for people the old market priced out. Because the bill never moved, this group kept its coverage.
